C9 The Canon · Reading Layer

Risk, Uncertainty & Fragility

Lesson Lectures · learn

Every plan you've ever made quietly assumed the future would behave like the past. The thinkers in this cluster say that assumption is exactly what blows you up. Risk you can measure; uncertainty you can't — and the rare, unmeasurable event is usually the one that decides everything. This lesson hands you two opposite-looking responses that turn out to be partners. From Nassim Taleb: stop trying to predict the catastrophe — re-engineer your exposure so the catastrophe can't kill you and the lucky break can make you. From Philip Tetlock: where the world is scoreable, forecasting is a learnable skill, not a gift. Tap the cards, the diagrams, and the quizzes as you go.

1 · The one idea: you can't predict the shock, so shape your exposure to it

Nassim Taleb spent 22 years as a derivatives trader before he wrote a word of philosophy, and his whole project starts from one trader's instinct: the average doesn't matter — the tail does. In The Black Swan (2007) he names the events that run history — rare, high-impact, and only obvious in hindsight. You will never forecast when one hits. But you can almost always see whether you're exposed to one.

Don't predict the Black Swan → measure your exposure to it → cut the fatal exposures, keep the survivable ones

Taleb's deeper move is to define the problem mathematically. Fragility isn't bad luck — it's a shape: a nonlinear, accelerating reaction to shocks, where a big hit hurts far more than many small ones added together.

"You can define the fragile mathematically as something that does not like mistakes… a small shock has no impact, a large shock has much more impact, disproportionately large. If the market goes down 10% you lose vastly more money if you're negatively exposed to volatility than if it went down 10 times 1%."

— Denis The Bear, "Nassim Taleb Explains Antifragility in Under 5 Minutes" · in your corpus

That convex-downside shape is Black Swan exposure. Ordinary "bell-curve" models price the little shocks correctly and quietly ignore the one in the tail that breaks you. The constructive sequel, Antifragile (2012), asks the question that names this whole shelf: what's the opposite of fragile?

2 · The triad — fragile, robust, antifragile

Ask most people for the opposite of "fragile" and they say "robust" or "resilient." Taleb says that's the wrong answer — it's like saying the opposite of negative is neutral. The true opposite isn't something that survives disorder; it's something that gains from it.

"If I'm sending a package to Siberia, fragile means handle with care. The opposite would not be 'I don't really care' — it would be 'likes disorder: shake me, I'll benefit from it.' There's a category of object like that without a word in the dictionary."

— Denis The Bear, "Nassim Taleb Explains Antifragility in Under 5 Minutes" · in your corpus

The corpus pins the triad with Norse imagery: the god Baldur — invulnerable except to the one overlooked mistletoe — is fragile; the boar Sæhrímnir, eaten every night and resurrected every morning, is robust; the Vikings themselves, who welcomed wounds because dying in battle bought entry to Valhalla, are antifragile. Tap each tier to see how it reacts to a shock.

Because antifragility has a dosage limit and is domain-specific. Muscle overcompensates after a heavy deadlift — but a car crash doesn't make the car stronger, it totals it. The Swedish Investor is explicit: the YouTuber gains from bad reputation but not from physical harm; the Viking gains from wounds but not from a ruined name. The stressor must be small relative to your recovery capacity. Too much volatility doesn't toughen you — it just kills you. This is the caveat Taleb's polemic tone tends to undersell, and the reason a startup can die from the very stress meant to harden it.

3 · Naive interventionism — how we manufacture fragility

Here's the trap that makes the modern world fragile: we treat all volatility as a defect to be engineered away. Taleb calls smothering a system's necessary stressors naive interventionism (the Swedes, charmingly, call it doing someone a "bear favor" — trying to help and causing more harm).

"Using hand antiseptics and staying away from public places… will deprive your immune system, which is antifragile, from stressors, causing it to be weaker in the long run… There's this central illusion in life that we can remove randomness by removing randomness. We can't — we just build up something fragile and pay greater consequences in the future."

— The Swedish Investor, "Antifragile Summary (by Nassim Taleb)" · in your corpus

The same pattern runs through over-protected kids, over-sterilized immune systems breeding allergies, antibiotic overuse breeding resistant bacteria, and "too big to fail" bailouts that let small fragilities grow into systemic ones. The cure is via negativa — improve by removing (a single point of failure, an over-leveraged dependency, a buffer-killing "efficiency"), not by adding another layer of control. And the corpus is honest about the over-correction: "positive antifragile systems are often better left alone." Sometimes the most useful intervention is none.

4 · The barbell — the answer to the Black Swan problem

So if you can't predict the shock, how do you build for it? Taleb's answer is the barbell: combine extreme safety with a small, capped-downside, uncapped-upside bet — and deliberately leave the fragile middle empty. You replicate the convex shape on purpose. The Swedish Investor calls this the resolution of the entire cluster.

"Predicting future events isn't possible, and largely irrelevant, as long as you can control your exposure to them… Put a large chunk of your portfolio in hyper-conservative investments and a smaller chunk in hyper-aggressive ones."

— The Swedish Investor, "Antifragile Summary (by Nassim Taleb)" · in your corpus

The safe end protects you from the negative Black Swan; the aggressive end gives you optionality — exposure to a positive one. The corpus' worked case: a friend warns that 80% of biotech startups fail in year one and only 5% survive five years. The friend forgets the convex payoff — hitting one of that top 5% can return tens of thousands of percent. Capped loss, open upside. Tap each end of the barbell.

5 · The vocabulary — flip to learn

The exact terms the canon uses. Tap a card to flip it.

6 · The counterweight — Tetlock and the scoreable world

Taleb says stop predicting. But not everything is a once-a-century earthquake. Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner's Superforecasting (2015) shows that on specific, time-bound, resolvable questions — "will this policy pass by Q3?" — most expert predictions are barely better than chance, yet a measurable minority are consistently better, and what they do is learnable. The first move is to swap certainty for a number.

"Forecasting works best when uncertainty is expressed as a number, as using numbers makes commitments explicit. Calibration means that your eighty percent calls should occur about eighty percent of the time, not just feeling confident. Resolution is important too, because staying near fifty-fifty avoids being wrong but also avoids being useful."

— MindScience 360, "Why Predictions Fail | Use Probabilities Instead of Certainty" · in your corpus

The method has a recognizable spine: start with the outside view (the base rate — "count similar past votes"), adjust with the inside view (the specifics of this case), then update incrementally as evidence arrives, and keep score with a Brier score so reality can teach you. Superforecasters are foxes: "intellectual humility… highly curious and open-minded… their ability to think probabilistically" (POCKETUNI). The reason almost nobody develops the skill is brutal and ordinary:

"In a tournament question with a clear deadline, one person posts sixty percent repeatedly and never learns much. Another person revises from forty to fifty-five to seventy as facts change, and the score reflects that learning… In most organizations, forecasts are made and forgotten, so there is no measurement, no revision, and no improvement."

— MindScience 360, "Why Predictions Fail" · in your corpus

So the two halves of the cluster aren't rivals — they're a division of labor. Survive-first (Taleb) for the fat-tailed exposures you can't score; forecast-better (Tetlock) for the recurring, resolvable calls you can. One quiet caveat from the corpus: Tetlock's own later work shows people run different rationalities — the "intuitive Economist," "Theologian," and "prosecutor" — so a clean probability is only one worldview, and sacred-value questions resist being reduced to a number.

7 · Putting it together: a stressor you can survive is a teacher

The most human version of antifragility in the corpus isn't a portfolio — it's a story about reps to failure. FightMediocrity, barred from owning a car at the Air Force Academy, decided to knock on every door asking to borrow one, absorbing rudeness and ridicule along the way.

"The more doors I knocked on, the more awkward situations I put myself in… the less I started to give a [—]… I wasn't a glass that was going to break, I wasn't simply resisting being broken — I was turning into a diamond with every door that I knocked on."

— FightMediocrity, "How to Build Mental Toughness — Antifragile by Nassim Taleb" · in your corpus

Worked example — launching a side project. You want to start a business but you're afraid of failing in public. Run it as a barbell, not a bet-the-house gamble. Safe end: keep the day job — that's your "never lose money," the buffer that makes a flop survivable. Convex end: ship many cheap, small experiments (MVPs, cold outreach, a dozen landing pages) where each failure costs little but a single hit could change your life — optionality. Via negativa: before adding features, remove the one dependency that could sink you (a single supplier, one client who's 70% of revenue). Tetlock layer: for each launch, write a number — "60% we get 100 sign-ups in 30 days" — log it, and check it after the deadline so your judgment actually compounds. Each awkward "door" you knock on is the survivable stressor turning the glass into a diamond. FightMediocrity's own line: it's "a lot easier to go to failure on your set in the gym than to go door to door" — so train the harder rep on purpose.

8 · Check yourself

What is the true opposite of "fragile," per Taleb?

Robust and resilient merely survive disorder. The genuine opposite of something that's harmed by volatility is something that benefits from it — "shake me, I'll benefit from it." Resilience is the ceiling for robustness, not the opposite of fragile.

Why does Taleb say "predicting future events is largely irrelevant"?

You can't predict when a plane crashes, but you can see that it can — so you screen for weapons. Focusing on exposure (cutting fatal downside, buying optionality) makes the unforecastable timing irrelevant. That's the barbell logic.

A forecaster who posts "60%" on every question and never moves it is failing at:

Staying near a flat number "avoids being wrong but also avoids being useful." The superforecaster revises 40 → 55 → 70 as facts change and keeps score — that updating loop, fed by a scorecard, is the skill.

⚠️ "Stress makes you stronger" has a dosage limit — and a domain

The seductive misread of this cluster is "embrace all chaos." Antifragility is bounded: the heavy deadlift builds muscle, but the car crash totals the car; the YouTuber gains from haters but not from prison. The stressor must be small relative to your recovery capacity, and it's domain-specific — gaining in one dimension says nothing about another. Apply it to a startup naively and the "toughening" stress just kills you before the upside arrives. And don't over-correct in the other direction either: Taleb's polemic oversells "everything robust is bad," but some systems — bridges, payroll, your safe-end allocation — should just be reliable. Use the barbell to keep fatal stressors away from the things that must not break, and reserve volatility for the convex end where you can afford to lose.

🔎 One subtlety → your bridge to the rest of the shelf

Notice the throughline that unites Taleb and Tetlock: both refuse the comfortable lie of certainty. Taleb attacks it from the tail (you can't know the rare event, so build to survive it); Tetlock attacks it from the middle (you can do better than chance, but only if you keep score). The deepest skill here isn't computing a probability or drawing a payoff curve — it's recognizing which kind of question you're in: a scoreable, repeatable one where calibration pays, or a fat-tailed one where survival is the only move. That single distinction is the hidden engine under investing (margin of safety), strategy (asymmetric bets), and leadership under crisis — where the cost of pretending you knew is paid by everyone downstream of you.

🎯 Your move

Do two things this week. (1) Find one fragility in your setup — a single point of failure, an over-leveraged dependency, the one client or supplier you can't survive losing — and apply via negativa: remove it, or build the safe-end buffer that makes its loss survivable. Then place one barbell bet: capped downside, uncapped upside (a cheap experiment that could pay off big). (2) Make one real forecast as a number — "65% we hit the deadline," not "probably." Write it down with a date. When it resolves, check it. Repeat. That loop — survive-first on the tails, keep-score on the middle — is the entire cluster in practice.

📚 Taught from these sources in your corpus

  • Denis The Bear — Nassim Taleb Explains Antifragility in Under 5 Minutes (fragility as nonlinearity; the definition by negation)
  • FightMediocrity — How to Build Mental Toughness: Antifragile by Nassim Taleb (the door-knocking diamond)
  • MindScience 360 — Why Predictions Fail | Use Probabilities Instead of Certainty (calibration, resolution, Brier scores)

ANTIFRAGILE SUMMARY (BY NASSIM TALEB)
The Swedish Investor · 20:51 · 287,589 views · Watch ↗
Read transcript · ~3,456 words

What do Vikings, the multiplying smartphone and YouTubers have in common? They're all antifragile. This is a top 5 takeaway summary of the fourth book in the Incerto series - Antifragile- Things That Gain From Disorder, written by Nassim Taleb. I will post a playlist consisting of all the books in the series in the description. We will now examine what antifragility is; how we as humans sometimes intervene too much with randomness, turning us fragile in the process; how one can detect what is antifragile; why antifragility is the solution to the Black Swan problem; and lastly, what we can learn from an isometric strategy named after a barbell.

Takeaway number 1: Introducing the triad - Fragile, Robust, Antifragile. To understand what antifragility is, we will now look at the triad. All good things come in three, right? Antifragility exists on a spectrum together with that which is robust and that which is fragile. The difference between the three of them lies in how they react to randomness, uncertainty, stressors, errors and most importantly, time. The fragile breaks when faced with uncertainty. The robust doesn't care too much, and the antifragiel - and here comes the central point of the book - becomes stronger. Let's take an example.

In Norse mythology, the god Baldur was protected from almost all harm, when his father Odin tried to have every creature and living thing swear an oath not to harm his son. The issue was that he forgot about the mistletoe. And so the evil god Loki made an arrow of the plant and later killed Baldur with it. Baldur, in this example, represents that which is fragile to physical harm. Another famous creature from the Nordic folklore is the boar Sæhrímnir. In Valhalla, it said that the Vikings killed the boar every evening and feasted on its meat. But every next morning, the boar was resurrected. Clearly it was robust - no matter how much physical damage the boar took from bacon-loving Vikings, it lived to see another day.

As an example of antifragility, take the Vikings themselves. They thought that dying in battle would give them the entrance to Valhalla. So being wounded wasn't something they were afraid of. This made it so they had an advantage in fighting the fragile Englishman and Frenchman. Another example ... Have you ever dropped a smartphone on a surface other than perhaps your bed door a really soft carpet? This is different than from back in the days when cellphones could take basically any physical damage. Although it hasn't been invented yet, we can imagine what the antifragile smartphone would be like.

Picture yourself throwing your phone in the ground, only to see it multiplied into two brand new phones, upgraded with all the latest software and gadgets. Wouldn't that be awesome? Okay, final example! Take the stressor of bad reputation and the effect it has on your career depending on which profession you've chosen. If you've chosen to climb the corporate ladder, you are fragile in this aspect. Any mistake you make will go into your permanent record at the personnel department, and could possibly harm your prospects at the workplace. Now, take the self-employed cab driver in a large city. It doesn't matter to him if he makes a mistake with one client, he can just go and pick up one of the other, million potential customers who doesn't know a thing about how he performed during his last drive.

And finally take the YouTuber. The YouTuber is antifragile to bad reputation. The more people hate, the more we earn. Not only do negative comments and thumbs down boost the YouTube algorithm, but think about word to mouth as well. I don't know how many times I've been recommended to watch something on the basis of how horrible, cringy, crazy or just plain bad it supposedly was. So the antifragile is something that likes randomness, uncertainty, stressors, errors, and time, because it gains from it. Antifragility is domain-specific though. The Vikings didn't gain much from bad reputation, and the YouTuber doesn't really enjoy physical harm.

Also, antifragility often only works up to a certain point. A Youtuber who gets such bad reputation that he goes to jail can't be said to have gained from it, I guess. Next we shall see how intervention can turn something antifragile into something fragile. Takeaway number 2: Naive interventionism (or bear favors, as we say in Sweden) What do soccer moms, your colleague who uses hand antiseptics all day, and the politicians who are bailing out banks, have in common? That's right, they are turning the antifragile into something fragile. Kids don't need protection from every potential harm in life, and neither do they need help overcoming every obstacle.

The personal development of an individual is antifragile to harm and obstacles (up to a certain point) or in other words, it gains from it! Removing these stressors from one's childhood, on the other hand, is likely to create a very weak and fragile adult. Similarly, using hand antiseptics and staying away from public places because you imagine that you might catch a disease otherwise, will deprive your immune system, which is antifragile, from stressors, causing it to be weaker in the long run. The removal of such stressors is likely the reason why allergies and autoimmune diseases plague our society today, and the antiseptics, together with the overuse of antibiotics, is strengthening the antifragile bacteria, creating antibiotic resistance.

Finally, we have the economists and the politicians who are intervening in the economy by deeming something "too big to fail" and therefore refusing to let nature take its course. Weeding out vulnerable firms early allows for minimal harm to the system, as they would otherwise grow to cause systemic problems. Nassim Taleb refers to this as "naive interventionism". In sweden, we call it "doing someone a bear favor" In plain English it's called "trying to help but causing more harm than good", or "fixing things that rather should be left alone". There's this central illusion in life that randomness is a bad thing, and that we can remove randomness by removing randomness.

The truth is that we can't, we will just build up something that is fragile and pay greater consequences in the future. Takeaway number 3: Concavity and convexity - detecting what is fragile and antifragile This is going to be a bit technical, but there's a way of detecting that which is fragile and that which is antifragile. Let's start with the fragile. Imagine yourself driving a car. You find parking quite difficult, so occasionally, you bump into stuff when parking the car, like neighboring cars, walls, road signs, slow pedestrians ... You've lost count on how many times this has happened, but when you add up the scratches in the car paints a quick estimation says ... maybe 20 times?

You didn't go faster than perhaps 5 km/h (about 3 miles per hour) in any of the accidents. Now imagine yourself driving that car into a wall in 5 * 20, 100 kilometres per hour (or about 60 miles per hour) a single time. Will it have the same effect on your car? Clearly not. Your car is fragile. The harm is not linear to the stressor, ie the velocity of the impact. Hitting a wall at 5 km/h 20 times will cause a lot of scratches. Hitting it in 100 km/h gives the vehicle a straight way ticket to the car cemetery. Mathematically, this can be shown by a non linear relationship on a graph and a so called "concave" function.

The antifragile is also detectable by its nonlinear response to a given stressor. But in this case, the function is "convex" instead. In other words, it responds positively to the stressor, and more so if you increase the intensity of it (up to a certain point). Muscle growth is antifragile to physical exhaustion. Lifting 100 kilos in deadlift for a single repetition is more beneficial than lifting 10 kilos 10 times. Average shmaverage, an interesting property follows from these concave and convex functions. It's much more important to understand the variance in the underlying variable X, in many situations, than to understand the average of it.

An illustration from personal experience: My mother has always been keen on arriving early to airports, so that one has a marginal safety and can make it in time for the flight, even if something unforeseen should happen. Me, on the other hand, have always thought of this as wasteful. Waiting an extra hour at the airport?? Forget about it! Then, last summer, when I was scheduled to fly to Prague in the Czech Republic I ... missed my flight. There were no other flights to Prague that day, and I really wanted to go. So instead .. well, I took the bus. Sure. It's a bit annoying having to wait for an hour at the airport every time you travel somewhere, but the annoyance of missing your flight and having to sit on an uncomfortable bus for 20 hours, exceeds that by a non-comparable magnitude.

Another example, of the opposite situation. You are being told that investing in early biotech companies is a bad idea. One of your friends argues so, and tells you that: "80% of biotech startups fail already within the first year, you know. 15% fail within 5 years, and yeah, I think only 5% managed to survive more than 5!" What your friend forgets about in this case is the non-linear relationship that exists between the survival of the company and the return for you as a stock owner. This is a convex function. Hitting a single one of these companies that belong to the top 5%, may have you settled for life, as returns can be in the tens of thousands of percentages.

If you want to hear more about this, head over to my summary of "Angel - How to Invest in Technology Startups". There's another way to detect what is likely to be fragile, and what is likely to be antifragile, and it's determined by the so called Lindy effect. (But more on that in the 2nd video) Take away number 4: The answer to the Black Swan problem First, a quick recap of what a Black Swan event is. It's unpredictable, and has a large impact. The impact is so big that Nassim Taleb argues that society to a large extent is decided by the outcome of these events. Negative Black Swans cause a lot of trouble, so it would be optimal if it was possible to foresee them.

But well, that's the issue with the unpredictable. It's ... not possible to predict. What's far easier though, is to see if a system is exposed to Black Swans. We do realize that, if an airplane crashes, all of the people on board will die. We can't foresee exactly WHEN and HOW that will happen, but we do understand that it CAN happen. So what can we do about it? We can try to change the system from being a fragile one, into being a robust or an antifragile one. By focusing on exposure to failure, we make the predictions about the failure largely irrelevant. Back to the example of airplanes. We check people for weapons before they board a plane.

Not because we think they carry weapons, but because the harm we expose ourselves to if we don't do so is too big. Remember, the concave property of the fragile systems from the last takeaway? The checking of people increases the effort for the airplane personnel, but it's not comparable to the price that the passengers have to pay, should the accident be there. In a fragile system, we introduce redundancy to reduce the fragility. Nature understands this well. For instance - humans have two kidneys, two breasts, two testicles (if male) fat reserves, etc, etc. Also, we are antifragile in that our body overcompensates to stressors.

If you do one rep on 100 kilos in deadlift your body will prepare you for lifting 110 kilos the next time. Humans don't understand this as well as nature does unfortunately. We tend to remove redundancy for the sake of "efficiency". We also tend to expect that the worst that we've seen is the worst possible outcome of the future as well. This is one of the reasons why so many blew up in the stock market in October 1987, when it crashed by 22% in a single day. The worst return from a single day up until that point was in October 1929, with the comparative minor crash of 12%. Warren Buffett is famous for having redundancy in his investments.

He suggests that one should: "Invest only in businesses that are so wonderful that an idiot can run them. Because sooner or later, one will." The difference between good and bad systems, is this the good systems are set up to have small errors, independent from each other. In fact, the mistakes are even negatively correlated to one another, as we tend to learn from them. For the investor, it's therefore a good idea to have uncorrelated bets. A portfolio consisting of only stocks from the energy sector, for instance, is fragile to the Black Swan event that a new competitor enters the market with an innovation that beats the living h*** out of the current technologies available.

Like ... energy made from a small portable fusion reactor or something like that. Furthermore, an antifragile or robust system often have options. Consider evolution, perhaps the best example there is of an antifragile system. Individuals die and even whole species go extinct from time to another. The surviving genes are "better" than the ones that go extinct - survival of the fittest. How can nature do this? It's because of optionality. If the dinosaurs can't handle the current situation, maybe the mammals can? Optionality can be introduced into ones investment strategy. Benjamin Graham famously invested in companies where the business was valued lower than the value of its assets.

Such an investment gives optionality. There's a chance that the company will do well, and in that case, it's awesome. If the business doesn't do well though, the company can still be liquidated, and the shareholders would keep a large part of their initial invested capital anyways. Takeaway number 5: The barbell strategy The barbell strategy consists of securing oneself of huge losses, while, at the same time, have an exposure to a large potential upside. It's the strategy of replicating the convex function from takeaway number 3. Let's see how females in some species use this approach, and how you can use it (whether female or not) in your choice of occupation and when investing.

In some monogamous species, including humans, females use this approach in choosing whom to mate with. They marry the stable and secure beta male, ie. securing the survival of their offspring, while they sometimes cheat with the alpha male, giving them a potential of securing the strongest genes to their offspring, at the same time. Minimizing downside, maximizing potential upside. When making your career decision, consider going for something conservative and something hyper aggressive at the same time. For instance. You can combine a 9-5 or an education with entrepreneurial endeavors in your spare time.

Or you can rely on safe investments to produce some income every month, just to put food on the table, while aggressively pursuing the entrepreneurial path with all your time and effort beyond that. In the field of finance, a lot of professionals misunderstand how to make profits over the long run. They believe that the focus should always be on coming up with bets that make them a lot of money. But what's most important is something different ... The difference appears minor, but it's not. What's most important is NOT to lose. Warren Buffett famously said: "The first rule of investing is: never lose money.

The second rule of investing is: never forget rule number one ." And if you don't take Buffett's word for it, consider that Ray Dalio, another one of the top 100 richest in the world, who also made his fortune from investing, says this: "Make sure that the probability of the unacceptable, ie. going bust, is nil" The barbell can be achieved by putting a large chunk of your portfolio in hyper conservative investments and a smaller chunk in hyper aggressive ones. I've discussed this previously in my summary of the Black Swan, which also is written by Nassim Taleb. Please check out that video if you're interested in hearing more about it.

There is a convex relationship between how many times you hear something and how long you can remember it for. Therefore - it's summary time! The antifragile becomes stronger from things such as randomness, uncertainty stressors and time. Positive antifragile systems are often better left alone. Fragility and antifragility can be detected by their nonlinear response to stressors. An interesting property of the nonlinear is that variance becomes much more important than averages. Predicting future events isn't possible, and largely irrelevant, as long as you can control your exposure to them. Use the barbel strategy to have the cake and eat it too.

And holy fu** ***** smokes, this book is awesome. Therefore, this will be one of the exceptions. This masterpiece by Nassim Taleb will consist of two videos, with ten takeaways in total. So if you've read the book before and you're like: "Swedish investor, are you crazy? Why isn't the Lindy effect included among your top five takeaways?" Patience. You'll have to wait until next week for part two. In the meantime, thanks for staying until the end of this video, and have a good one.

THE BLACK SWAN SUMMARY (BY NASSIM TALEB)
The Swedish Investor · 18:10 · 332,195 views · Watch ↗
Read transcript · ~3,002 words

Takeaway number one, the black swan problem. For an event to qualify as a black swan, it must fulfill the following three. One, it's an outlier. Nothing that has happened before can convincingly point to even the possibility of the event. Two, it carries an extreme impact. Three, it becomes explainable only after the fact. Human nature fools us into believing that we should have been able to know it would happen. all along. Other examples of black swans are the outbreak of World War I, 9/11, Black Monday, and the Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami. The black swan problem is also called the problem of induction.

The basic principle is that there are great uncertainties when trying to forecast the future given the knowledge of the past. How can we expect to be able to figure out the properties of something that is infinite and unknown based on something that is finite and known? Let's take another example, a textbook one. Imagine that you're a turkey living on a farm. From the day that you were born, some friendly creatures with two legs and two arms have been feeding you. Every day, they keep coming back with food. Also, they built a nice fence which protected you from that hairy thing on four legs, which look like it wanted to rip your guts out.

They even bring female turkeys to you occasionally. What lovely creatures they seem to be. For every passing day, as you are fed, protected, and stimulated, you become more and more certain that these must be the friendliest creatures on Earth. Until that day called Thanksgiving, when they're no longer so friendly anymore. Thanksgiving definitely came as a black swan for this turkey. From the point of view of the turkey, it was totally unexpected, had an extreme impact, and if he could have reasoned around the event after its occurrence, he might even have found explanations for it. From this, we can conclude that a black swan is a sucker's problem.

It's only a black swan if you're not informed. This goes for randomness in general. It's nothing else than lack of knowledge. For the turkey, him making it to the Thanksgiving table of some hungry human family was totally unexpected, but the family had probably known the exact date of the event for months. There's a cousin of the black swan, which is called the gray swan. This concerns the known unknowns, things that we know that we don't know. We don't know how fast a man can run 100 m, but we know that we don't know that. A black swan on the other hand is an unknown unknown. We don't even know that we don't know that.

Imagine a book that you have never read and that you haven't watched a summary of on my channel. Of course, that contains a lot of unknown unknowns. If you decide to read the book one day, at some point you'll exclaim, "Oh, I didn't know that." But you can't foresee today what content you'll be exclaiming that about. Takeaway number two, the implications of black swan blindness. Nasim Taleb talks about five related issues to the black swan that emerge from our blindness to it. I've discussed some of these previously in my summary of thinking fast and slow. One, the error of confirmation. We as humans are prone to draw conclusions from what we've seen to the unseen.

For instance, I've heard a strange argument regarding if graduating from college is a good idea or not. It goes something like this. Well, Bill Gates, Thomas Edison, Richard Branson, and and many other billionaires are school dropouts. Let's exaggerate a bit. Even if we pretend that all billionaires are school dropouts, we can never, I repeat, never, conclude the opposite from that statement that all school dropouts are billionaires. That billionaires are school dropouts doesn't confirm that it's a good idea to drop out from school. Yet, using it as an argument for leaving school is not uncommon, but the argument is flawed at best.

Two, the narrative fallacy. Last year, a friend of mine and I went to Australia for a few weeks of vacation. We went to this kind of remote place called Mission Beach, and the only reason for going there is basically skydiving and rafting. We had our eyes set on skydiving, but uh not for long. A friendly fella at our hostel told us about an accident which had happened the week before. In a tandem skydive, the parachute of the tandem jumpers and that of their cameraman had apparently twisted around each other during the jump, which caused all three of them to fall to their deaths. Me and my friend went rafting instead.

It didn't matter that when I asked my friend Siri, he told me that I was very unlikely to die in a skydive. Hey Siri, what's the risk of dying in a skydive? Here's what I found on the web. What's the risk of dying in a sky dive? Have a look. Stories stick. Statistics do not. This is the narrative fallacy. Sorry for making you less likely to go skydiving. Three, we are not programmed for black swans. Humans are prone to believe in linear progression. We think that a certain input will gradually result in a desired output. Not so when black swans exist. Imagine the author who's been spending many years writing books.

After 10 years of intensely hard work, she finally has her first book published and it becomes a blockbuster. That's a typical black swan event. Her effort to progression curve looked something like this. Not even remotely resembling the linear progression which would have looked something like this. Imagine how demoralizing the first 9 years must have been for this author. as all her friends expected that her progress would look something like this. While it actually looked like this four, the distortion of silent evidence. History has a tendency of hiding black swans for us by filtering the reality that we are presented with.

Consider the sailors of the 15th century that came back after their voyages to tell that they survived through many storms through praying together. Does this imply that praying together makes it less likely for your ship to sink? Well, maybe. But we must also consider the rest of the sailors, those that didn't survive the voyages. Did they pray or well, did they not? We may never know because they can't really tell us from the bottom of the ocean. Five, tunneling. We tend to focus too much on what we know and shy away from what we don't know. For instance, school teaches us many models on how to interpret reality.

Many of the inventors of these models were great thinkers. Yet, they can't think outside the box of their own models. And sometimes being too narrow and relying too much on these models can be devastating for the interpretation of the real world. as we shall see in takeaway number four. Takeaway number three, mediocran versus extremistan. Let's explore two new countries, shall we? Starting with mediocran from Goththingberg to Medioan. Search. Mediocristan is the land of the average. In mediocran, the first 100 observations of a variable will give you a good expectation of what you might see for the say next 1,000 observations.

The supreme law of this country is as follows. When your sample size is large, no single instance will significantly change the aggregate or the total. For instance, weight, height, mortality rates, car accidents, and the salary of a college graduate. uh in Sweden are all matters that belong to mediocran. Consider the total height of the people in a sample of 100 Swedish males. Let's pretend that their total length is 182 m using 182 cm per person, which is the height of the average Swedish male. Now, let's add the world's tallest man in history to the sample, Robert Wadllo, who was a staggering 272 cm tall.

The total length is now 184.7 m, which is an increase of about 1.5%. Not too radical, right? Now, let's buy a lastminute ticket and travel to extreistan instead. Extreme. In extremist, we introduce black swans. This makes it so that the first 100 observations might not give so much information about the next 1,000 ones at all. Remember the life of the turkey. His first 100 days of being fed and protected by humans couldn't really tell him that he was about to become Thanksgiving dinner on the 101st day. Most human-made or social matters belong to extremistan such as wealth, income, book sales per author, number of subs per YouTuber, deaths in war, sizes of planets, and of course, financial markets.

Consider the total wealth of the people in a sample of 100 suites. Let's pretend that their total wealth is uh $19 million using $190,000 per person, which is the wealth of the average Swede. Now, let's add Warren Buffett to the sample, who currently has a net worth of $84.2 billion. The total wealth is now $84.22 billion, which is an increase of approximately 443,100%. That's quite the difference. The implications are as follows. In mediocran, we can safely do some predictions. In extremistan, it's much more difficult, maybe even impossible. Problems arise because we seem to think that we are living in mediocran.

While almost all of the matters that we're trying to forecast are matters of extremistan, sometimes we base important functions in our society around these predictions such as the banking system and that leads to economic crisis such as the financial crisis of 2007 to 2008. Takeaway number four, Gaussian. the bell curve or the normal distribution as we refer to it in school or the Gaussian curve as we refer to it when we think that we're honoring its original inventor Carl Fredish Gaus is a very common tool used for risk management among regulators and central bankers among others let's talk about what this curve is first and foremost its fundamental property is that data from a given random variable say height will hover around the average for instance Take the example of the Swedish males presented previously.

The average height is 182 cm. If you look at the likelihood that someone is taller than say 189 cm, you may see that only one out of 6.3 males are taller than 196 cm, 1 out of 44. Taller than 203 cm, one out of 740. What's important to notice here is not the actual numbers but that the same incremental increase in our random variable i.e. height leads to an even faster decline in its number of observations. You can say that the variable is experiencing everinccreasing headwind whenever it tries to deviate from the mean. Now the normal distribution is awesome when it's applied under the right conditions which is in mediocre. then our previous observations can tell a whole lot about potential future ones.

It does not work with variables from extremist though. For example, if you modeled daily stock market returns as normally distributed and you were faced with a black Monday of 1987 where the market crashed by 22.6% 6% in a single day. You would have to call this event an outlier because according to the normal distribution, it should only happen once in several billion lifetimes. Many investors went bankrupt because they didn't even consider the possibility of something like this happening. It was a black swan to them. So we see that the normal distribution can be limited nay dangerous to use for decision-m under circumstances when we deal with matters from extremistan.

And remember this is pretty much all humanmade social matters. Then the question becomes what can we do instead? We can use something Nasim Taleb calls mandelian randomness instead of pretending that everything is normally distributed. Mandelroian randomness does not assume that deviations from the mean becomes increasingly difficult. Instead, it suggests that for instance, if we talk about losses in a single day in the stock market, it's just as rare to see a day resulting in a return of -5% instead of -2.5%. As it is to see - 10%, rather than -5%. Going from -1.25 25 to -2.5 to -5 to -10 to -20 are all the same in terms of probability.

I mean if we would have assumed that on the Friday before the black Monday, we would at least have considered a minus 22.6% decline a possibility and we would have been able to protect ourselves from such an event. By assuming mandalian randomness instead of the normal distribution, we can turn some black swans into gray swans. Gray swans are known unknowns. As we discussed in the first takeaway, they are better than black swans because at least we can adapt our decision-m to something that we know that we don't know about. Takeaway number five, how to act as an investor in an environment of black swans.

And now to the most interesting part. In a world dominated by black swans, where we fool ourselves with the error of confirmation, the narrative fallacy and tunneling, and where we must be very careful when using the platonic normal distribution for anything useful. What should we do? Nasim Taleb suggests two different approaches. One, the hyperconservative and hyperaggressive approach. Don't put your money in some medium risk investments because let's face it, how do we know that it's medium risk anyways? Did some expert compute that using a normal distribution perhaps? Instead, put a majority of your money in something extremely safe like treasury bills.

These aren't hedged against black swans either, but if you lose your money in treasury bills, you'll have bigger problems than just losing your investment capital. [Applause] The rest of the money should be put in something extremely speculative like options or angel investments. With this type of portfolio, you are limited in your risk because of your hyperconervative investments, but you are also exposed to the possibility of hitting a positive black swan with your hyperaggressive ones. Nasim Taleb refers to this as a convex combination. Two, the speculative insured portfolio. The second option is to have a very speculative portfolio, but to ensure it against losses that are greater than, for example, 15%.

This might not always be possible, though, depending on what your portfolio consists of. Instead of using an actual insurance company, you can create this effect yourself by putting up stop- losses at minus 15% and taking multiple bets with small parts of your equity. This strategy is also convex. Your risk is limited, but your upside is exposed to positive black swans. This is by far the longest video I've made to date, so I think a summary is in place. Humans love to predict, but black swans make the future a little less certain than we'd like to think. From black swan blindness, many other themes arise like the error of confirmation, the narrative fallacy, silent evidence and tunneling.

We tend to think that we live in mediocran. But most of the matters in our society are belongings to extremistan. We must treat them accordingly. To use mandalian randomness in favor of the normal distribution can help us in turning some black swans into gray ones. In investing, Nasim Taleb suggests that we should expose ourselves to the possibility of positive black swans and limit our risk by decreasing our exposure to negative ones. Well, that's it for this time. I hope to see you again soon.

Why Predictions Fail | Use Probabilities Instead of Certainty
MindScience 360 · 8:20 · 24 views · Watch ↗

A briefing begins, confident voices promise certainty, and decisions are made before anyone questions the fragility of these predictions. Weeks later, the outcome surprises everyone, and the postmortem blames bad luck rather than flawed thinking. Forecasts fail because people treat complex systems as simple machines, then speak with certainties they cannot justify. The solution starts by replacing yes or no claims with probabilities, clear definitions, and timelines that can be verified. Better forecasting reduces avoidable surprises because plans can match realistic uncertainty rather than wishful confidence.

It also enhances learning, as every forecast becomes feedback on judgment, not just a headline. Imagine a team reviewing a geopolitical question, breaking it into parts, and assigning ranges instead of single dates. As new reports emerge, probability estimates adjust, and the team records what changed. Next, you will learn how good forecasters keep score, update their beliefs, and work in groups to improve accuracy. This video is inspired by Superforecasting by Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner, and please subscribe for practice using probabilities, updates, and scoring. Forecasting works best when uncertainty is expressed as a number, as using numbers makes commitments explicit.

Calibration means that your eighty percent calls should occur about eighty percent of the time, not just feeling confident. Resolution is important too, because staying near fifty-fifty avoids being wrong but also avoids being useful. Good forecasters adjust probabilities higher or lower when evidence warrants it, then accept the scoring consequences. In a tournament question with a clear deadline, one person posts sixty percent repeatedly and never learns much. Another person revises from forty to fifty-five to seventy as facts change, and the score reflects that learning. This approach treats forecasting as a measurable skill, not a mysterious gift reserved for famous pundits.

Once forecasts are numerical and testable, improvement becomes possible through feedback, comparison, and steady practice. Start by translating a confident statement into a probability range, then define what would count as a clear outcome. Keep a small log of your probabilities and dates, so you can later compare confidence with reality. A useful forecast starts with an outside view, which anchors your estimate to base rates from similar cases. Then, an inside view tests specific pathways, asking what must be true for each hypothesis to hold. Base rates prevent wild swings driven by the latest headline, especially when emotions tempt you to overreact.

Hypothesis checking reduces aimless information hunting, as evidence is gathered for and against each possibility. Consider a question about whether a policy will pass within a short window, and begin by counting similar past votes. Next, adjust that baseline for new factors like shifting alliances or public opinion, and compute a rough probability. This method keeps forecasts grounded, blending statistical reality with context instead of choosing one perspective. It also makes disagreements productive, as people can debate assumptions, base rates, and evidence rather than personalities. Write the question in precise terms, list two or three plausible pathways, and assign initial probabilities to each.

Update those numbers in small steps when new information appears, noting which assumption each update depended on. Forecasting improves only when accuracy is measured, as unscored judgments cannot teach you what works. A scoring rule rewards both calibration and decisive probabilities, while punishing overconfidence when certainty is wrong. Brier scores convert forecasts into distances from what happened, so lower scores mean closer contact with reality. Benchmarks matter because some questions are easy, and skill means beating simple rules and the crowd. Weather forecasters improve by making many predictions, checking them, and tweaking models in a repeating cycle.

In most organizations, forecasts are made and forgotten, so there is no measurement, no revision, and no improvement. Keeping score turns forecasting into evidence-based thinking, where methods are tested the way other crafts are tested. It also reduces the demand for confident narratives, as performance replaces reputation as the basis for trust. Pick a handful of questions with clear time frames, write probabilities now, and score yourself after the deadline passes. If keeping score feels empowering, please subscribe to keep learning how to measure judgment and update faster. Forecasting accuracy depends less on ideology and more on thinking style, especially how you handle complexity!

One style forces problems into a single Big Idea, while another shifts tools as the problem demands. The flexible style uses many small clues and transition words like but and however, which keeps doubt visible. That doubt is a feature, because it invites revision and reduces the urge to declare outcomes certain or impossible! A television pundit repeats one storyline across years and stays confident even as events contradict it. A careful forecaster gathers diverse sources, tests opposing evidence, and adjusts probability estimates when the balance shifts. Active open-mindedness treats beliefs as hypotheses to test, so disagreement becomes data rather than an identity threat.

This mindset fits probabilistic forecasting, because changing your mind is expected when the evidence changes! Build a habit of seeking one source that challenges your view, then write what would change your estimate. Practice saying I was wrong, then record the correction, because that single move protects you from stubborn stories! The most reliable edge is perpetual beta, a commitment to constant learning, self-checking, and belief updating. Superforecasters tend to be cautious and humble, thinking in many grades of maybe. They update thoughtfully, as when facts change, the forecast changes too, and the log captures the shift.

They also check cognitive and emotional biases, reducing impulsive leaps that feel smart in the moment. When forecasters work in teams, sharing assumptions and arguing respectfully, the group can outperform isolated individuals. Diverse perspectives help because different scraps of information combine, and the aggregated estimate can be pushed toward the truth. This shows why leadership matters, as organizations must balance collaboration, dissent, and incentives without sliding into groupthink. The goal is not harmony, but a culture where people challenge claims, share sources, and keep updating together.

Form a small forecasting circle, assign roles for base rates and counterarguments, then merge estimates into one number. After scoring, review what each person missed, treating the postmortem as training rather than blame. Forecasting is not fortune telling; it is disciplined judgment under uncertainty, practiced like any other skill. An optimistic skeptic accepts that certainty is rare but still believes accuracy can improve through method. You learned how probabilities, clear questions, and base rates create starting points that resist panic and hype. You also discovered why scoring, calibration, and repeated updating turn forecasts into feedback loops that compound.

Over time, this reduces costly overconfidence because decisions reflect realistic ranges and contingency plans are chosen earlier. It also changes group decisions because teams learn to debate assumptions, share evidence, and average wisely. Start with one forecast this week, write a number, and commit to revising only when new evidence appears. Then create a simple scorecard because measurement is the gate that turns guessing into improvement. If you maintain the perpetual beta mindset, each correction becomes progress, and humility becomes a competitive advantage. For more ways to practice these forecasting habits, please subscribe and keep building calibrated judgment in everyday decisions.
